In response to your comments, we have carefully revised the manuscript, conducted additional experiments, and refined our interpretations to strengthen the overall rigor and clarity of the study. Detailed point-by-point responses are provided below. Once again, we sincerely thank you for your valuable time, insightful comments, and efforts in helping us improve the quality of our work.
Major comments:
Q1: If the authors wish to show that T cells mediate the anti-tumor effect after inhibition of B7H3 palmitoylation, then at the very least the T cells should have been deleted.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this insightful and important suggestion. As recommended, we performed CD8⁺ T cell depletion experiments to determine whether the anti-tumor effect observed upon inhibition of B7H3 palmitoylation is mediated by CD8+ T cells. Specifically, anti-CD8α monoclonal antibody (mAb) was administered intraperitoneally one day prior to subcutaneous implantation of MC38 tumor cells, followed by two additional doses at weekly intervals (three injections in total) (Response Figure.1a; Fig. 3I in the manuscript). Strikingly, depletion of CD8⁺ T cells completely abolished the difference in tumor growth between wild-type B7H3 and the palmitoylation-deficient C278A mutant, indicating that the anti-tumor effect conferred by B7H3 palmitoylation deficiency is indeed CD8⁺ T cell-dependent (Response Figure.1b-d; Fig. 3J, 3K, and Fig. S3J in the manuscript). We truly appreciate your suggestion, which led us to perform this critical experiment and significantly enhanced the rigor and completeness of our study.
Response Figure.1 CD8⁺ T cell depletion abolishes the anti-tumor effect driven by B7H3 palmitoylation deficiency.
Q2: The result of Fig3G showed many immune cell populations (such as CD8+T, CD4+T, NKT, NK, MDSC and so on) were significantly changed by the inhibition of B7H3 palmitoylation, but only the CD8+T was discussed in the following research. The other populations should also be concerned.
Response: We sincerely thank you for the thoughtful and professional comment regarding the broader impact of B7H3 palmitoylation on various immune cell populations, as shown in Figure 3G. Firstly, among the immune subsets analyzed—including CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, NKT cells, NK cells, and MDSCs—the change in CD8⁺ T cells was the most pronounced following the loss of B7H3 palmitoylation, as shown in Figure 3G and 3H. Secondly, CD8⁺ T cells are widely recognized as the principal effectors that directly mediate tumor cell killing and play a pivotal role in shaping the overall effectiveness of antitumor immune responses[1, 2]. In line with this, numerous studies have demonstrated that both the abundance and functional state of CD8⁺ T cells serve as reliable indicators of effective antitumor immunity[3, 4]. Furthermore, B7H3 is a member of the B7 family, sharing structural and functional similarities with immune checkpoint molecules such as PD-L1[5]. Based on this analogy, we hypothesize that B7H3 palmitoylation, similar to PD-L1, regulates antitumor immunity primarily through its impact on CD8⁺ T cell function. To functionally validate the importance of CD8⁺ T cells in this context, we performed depletion experiments using CD8⁺ T-depleting antibodies, which revealed that the enhanced antitumor effects associated with B7H3 palmitoylation deficiency were abolished following CD8⁺ T cell removal, as shown in Response Figure 1. These results further underscore the indispensable role of CD8⁺ T cells in mediating the observed immune response. Taken together, these findings provide a rationale for our decision to center the mechanistic investigation on CD8⁺ T cells. While we fully acknowledge that other immune cell types, including CD4⁺ T cells, NKT cells, NK cells, and MDSCs, may also contribute meaningfully to the tumor immune microenvironment, we believe that prioritizing CD8⁺ T cells in this study is both scientifically sound and supported by our data. Once again, we are grateful to you for this valuable suggestion, which has helped us strengthen the depth and clarity of our work.
Reference:
[1] RASKOV H, ORHAN A, CHRISTENSEN J P, et al. Cytotoxic CD8+ T Cells in Cancer and Cancer Immunotherapy[J]. British Journal of Cancer, 2021, 124(2): 359–367.
[2] GILES J R, GLOBIG A M, KAECH S M, et al. CD8+ T Cells in the Cancer-Immunity Cycle[J]. Immunity, 2023, 56(10): 2231–2253.
[3] EJ W. T Cell Exhaustion[J]. Nature immunology, 2011, 12(6).
[4] HEGDE P S, CHEN D S. Top 10 Challenges in Cancer Immunotherapy[J]. Immunity, 2020, 52(1): 17–35.
[5] B Z, H L, Y X, et al. Immune Checkpoint of B7-H3 in Cancer: From Immunology to Clinical Immunotherapy[J]. Journal of hematology & oncology, 2022, 15(1).
Q3: Although cleaved caspase 3 looks good in both human and mouse in vitro co-culture systems, the overall survival data of tumor cells should be shown, for the tumor cells may not only undergo apoptosis.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comment. While cleaved caspase-3 staining provides clear evidence of apoptosis in both human and mouse in vitro co-culture systems, we fully agree that additional data assessing overall tumor cell survival are necessary. In fact, we had already performed LDH release assays in parallel with cleaved caspase-3 flow cytometry. LDH, as a stable cytosolic enzyme released upon loss of membrane integrity, reflects both apoptotic and necrotic cell death. These results have been presented in Figure 3T, Figure S5R, and Figure 6K. In addition, in response to your suggestion, we have now performed crystal violet staining to further assess the overall survival of tumor cells after T cell–mediated killing. Quantification of the remaining adherent tumor cells by absorbance at 570 nm revealed that both ZDHHC24 knockdown and the C496A mutation of B7H3 significantly enhanced CD8⁺ T cell–mediated tumor cell killing) (Response Figure.2). These findings provide further support for the functional relevance of B7H3 palmitoylation in immune evasion. We are grateful for your constructive feedback, which has helped us enhance the completeness and robustness of our study.
Response Figure.2 B7H3 C496A mutation and ZDHHC24 knockdown enhance CD8⁺ T cell–mediated tumor cell killing.
Q4: All the immunoblotting results in this study lack labels of protein molecular weight.
Response: We sincerely thank you for pointing this out. In response to your suggestion, we have carefully reviewed all the immunoblotting figures and have now added the appropriate protein molecular weight markers to each blot.
Q5: In the Fig4B, the background of IgG group is particularly clean compared with both Input and IP groups, and it seems like lack of protein sample. Please repeated this experiment and provide corresponding internal control protein.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful observation and valuable suggestion. We agree that the IgG group in the original Figure 4B appeared to have a particularly clean background compared to the Input and IP groups. We believe this was likely due to the relatively short incubation time (0.5h at room temperature) between the protein lysate and antibody-conjugated magnetic beads, which may have reduced nonspecific binding. Additionally, a shorter exposure time was used for this blot, which may have further contributed to the clean background. In response to your suggestion, we have repeated the Co-IP experiment with improved conditions. Specifically, we extended the incubation time between the antibody-conjugated beads and the lysates to 8 hours at 4°C and increased the exposure time during imaging. The updated results are now shown in the revised manuscript (Response Figure.3; Fig. 4A in the manuscript). Regarding the internal control protein, we would like to clarify that conventional housekeeping proteins such as GAPDH or β-actin are not typically suitable for Co-IP experiments. This is because Co-IP aims to detect specific protein–protein interactions from a limited immunoprecipitated fraction rather than from total lysates, and the sample input is not standardized in the same way as conventional Western blots. Therefore, internal loading controls like β-actin are generally not informative in this context. Instead, we included the IgG heavy chain as an internal reference to indicate successful immunoprecipitation. However, in specific experiments such as the pull-down of B7H3 using a rabbit anti-ZDHHC24 antibody, the corresponding IgG was also rabbit-derived. Since B7H3 was detected using a mouse primary antibody and an anti-mouse secondary antibody, the rabbit IgG heavy chain was not visualized on the blot. This is due to the species-specific detection in Western blot, where the anti-mouse secondary antibody does not recognize rabbit IgG. We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s attention to this detail, which prompted us to improve both the experimental design and the clarity of data presentation.
Response Figure 3. Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of the interaction between ZDHHC24 and B7H3.
Q6: In the FigS4a, Flag-ZDHHC9/ZDHHC16/ZDHHC22 did not successfully express after transfection, and whether they participate in the palmitoylation of B7H3 is unknown. Additional experiments are needed to rule out their effects.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this insightful comment. As suggested, we performed the transfection experiments for Flag-ZDHHC9, ZDHHC16, and ZDHHC22 to further assess their potential involvement in B7H3 palmitoylation. Although the expression of these constructs appeared weak in Figure S4a, we believe this is attributable to their inherently low expression levels and distinct subcellular localizations—ZDHHC9 localizes to the ER and Golgi, ZDHHC16 to the ER, and ZDHHC22 to both the ER and Golgi—which may reduce their detectability under our initial screening conditions. To clarify this, we individually transfected each of these ZDHHCs and examined their effects on B7H3 protein levels. Consistently, we did not observe any appreciable change in B7H3 expression following overexpression of ZDHHC9, ZDHHC16, or ZDHHC22 (Response Figure.4). Although ABE assays were not conducted in this specific follow-up experiment, our previous data have established a strong correlation between B7H3 palmitoylation and its protein stability. Therefore, the lack of effect on B7H3 levels suggests that these ZDHHC enzymes are unlikely to catalyze its palmitoylation. We appreciate your suggestion, which prompted us to further validate the specificity of ZDHHC24 in regulating B7H3 palmitoylation.
Response Figure 4. Evaluation of ZDHHC9, ZDHHC16, and ZDHHC22 in regulating B7H3 expression.
Q7: Some of the flow cytometry analyses only provide statistical charts, and the mode charts should also be shown.
Response: We sincerely thank you for the thoughtful comment. We quiet understand the importance of including representative flow cytometry plots to support quantitative analyses. For all flow cytometry-based experiments presented in the manuscript, representative plots (mode charts) have already been included alongside the corresponding statistical summaries. Specifically, these representative plots can be found in the following figures: Main Figures – Fig. 6G, Fig. 6I, Fig. 8J, Fig. 8L; Supplementary Figures – Fig. S3L–O, Fig. S5K, S5N–P, Fig. S6C, S6E, Fig. S7F, Fig. S8N, Fig. S9C–E. In addition, for the newly added figures in this version of the manuscript, we have also included the corresponding representative flow cytometry plots where appropriate (Fig. S1C, Fig. 8R, Fig. 8T, and Fig. 8V). Furthermore, we have provided gating strategy plots in the supplementary Figures S10 and S11.We have carefully reviewed all relevant figures again to ensure that the flow cytometry plots are clearly presented and appropriately labeled. We would be pleased to provide any further plots or clarifications that could assist in the review. Thank you again for pointing this out.
Reviewer #2:
This study reveals a novel mechanism underlying the lower response rate to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy in microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC) patients compared to microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) patients, highlighting the role of B7-H3 overexpression in tumor cells. Using patient tumor tissue samples and multi-omics technologies such as transcriptomics and metabolomics, they discovered that B7-H3 expression is significantly higher in MSS patient tissues compared to MSI patients. Furthermore, they elucidated that the key molecular mechanism involves palmitic acid-mediated palmitoylation modification of B7-H3. In detail, they discovered that ZDHHC24 mediates the palmitoylation of B7H3 at Cys496, which hinders its interaction with autophagy cargo receptor-p62 to inhibit its protein degradation. Based on their molecular mechanism, they designed a small mimic peptide of B7H3, which can enhance CD8+ T cell function by blocking the interaction between ZDHHC24 and B7H3. This strategy also elevated the sensibility and responsibility of CRC cells to the ICB therapy. Overall, this study is highly interesting and innovative, with rigorous experimental design and reliable results. It offers new perspectives and a material foundation for tackling the unresponsiveness of most CRC patients to ICB therapy in clinical settings.
Response: We sincerely thank you for the thoughtful and comprehensive evaluation of our manuscript. We are especially grateful for your appreciation of the novelty and scientific rigor of our study, as well as the translational relevance of our findings. Your encouraging comments on our experimental design, multi-omics analyses, and therapeutic strategy targeting B7H3 palmitoylation are deeply appreciated and highly encouraging. At the same time, we highly value the constructive suggestions regarding the limitations of our work. Your insights have guided several important improvements that have further strengthened the clarity and impact of the manuscript. Thank you again for your time, support, and helpful feedback.
Major comments:
Q1: As an immune checkpoint, B7-H3 not only expresses in tumor cells, but also in immune cells, including monocytes, dendritic cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), neutrophils, macrophages, B cells, and activated T cells. So, is B7H3 only highly expressed in tumor cells of MSS type tumor tissues? The author didn’t make any exclusion experiments. If not, does the molecular mechanism also suit in other immune cells?
Response: We sincerely thank you for your important and insightful comment. We fully agree that B7H3 can be expressed not only in tumor cells but also in various immune cell populations. In response to this important point, we conducted additional experiments using freshly collected clinical tumor samples. We performed immunofluorescence staining with EPCAM (a tumor cell marker, in green) and B7H3 (in red, Cy5), and observed extensive co-localization of EPCAM and B7H3 in tumor tissues, indicating that B7H3 is predominantly expressed in tumor cells (Response Figure.5a; Fig. S1B in the manuscript). Furthermore, flow cytometry analysis revealed that while approximately 30% of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment are B7H3-positive, the B7H3 positivity rate in tumor cells is more than 95% (Response Figure.5b-c; Fig. S1C-S1D in the manuscript). When normalized to 100,000 total cells, the number of B7H3⁺ tumor cells were estimated to be around 90,000 (Response Figure.5d; Fig. S1E in the manuscript), further supporting the notion that tumor cells are the dominant source of B7H3 expression in the MSS tumor context. While we do not exclude the possibility that the molecular mechanism we proposed could also be relevant in immune cells, we believe that, within the tumor microenvironment, the overwhelming expression of B7H3 in tumor cells suggests that the described palmitoylation-dependent regulatory mechanism primarily functions in tumor cells. We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion, which prompted us to perform these additional validations and helped further strengthen the conclusions of our study.
Response Figure 5. B7H3 expression is predominantly localized to tumor cells in MSS colorectal cancer tissues.
Q2: The authors explored their molecular mechanism mainly in RKO cells (MSI), SW480 cells (MSS), CT26 cells (MSS) and MC38 cells (MSI). I wonder whether B7H3 is also highly expressed in MSS CRC cell lines compared to the MSI ones. If this post-translational modification of B7-H3 exists in both MSS and MSI-type tumor cells, then is the high expression of B7-H3 in MSS tissues primarily due to differences in ZDHHC24 expression or the distribution of palmitic acid, or both? If it is due to ZDHHC24, they should provide more details of its protein expression in MSS and MSI tumor tissues and cells. If it is due to palmitic acid, it would be interesting to know why there is a higher abundance of palmitic acid in MSS tumors. At least, it could be a good content for the discussion part.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful and insightful comment. In response to your suggestion and to further improve the completeness of our study, we examined the expression of B7H3 and ZDHHC24 in a panel of human colorectal cancer cell lines representing both MSS and MSI-H subtypes. Notably, we did not observe consistent differences in the protein levels of B7H3 or ZDHHC24 between MSS and MSI-H cell lines (Response Figure.6a; Fig. S4L in the manuscript). However, analysis of patient-derived tumor tissues revealed that ZDHHC24 expression is significantly elevated in MSS tumors compared to MSI-H tumors (Response Figure.6b; Fig. S4M in the manuscript). This discrepancy between cell lines and clinical samples may reflect the influence of the in vivo tumor microenvironment, which is absent in standard in vitro models. In addition to the elevated expression of ZDHHC24, our metabolomic profiling showed that palmitic acid abundance is also higher in MSS tumors than in MSI-H tumors (Fig. 1D in the manuscript). These findings suggest that both increased ZDHHC24 expression and enhanced palmitic acid availability may cooperatively promote B7H3 palmitoylation and stabilization in MSS tumors. We have expanded the Discussion section to explore potential mechanisms underlying the elevated palmitic acid levels observed in MSS tumors (Page 19-20, line 565-576). We are grateful for this valuable suggestion, which helped us refine our interpretation and explore a broader biological context for our findings.
Response Figure 6. Expression of B7H3 and ZDHHC24 in colorectal cancer cell lines and ZDHHC24 expression in patient tumor tissues.
Q3: Whether ZDHHC24 enhances the protein stability of B7H3 should be detected.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this insightful comment, which helped us further improve the completeness of our study. Following your suggestion, we performed additional experiments to investigate whether ZDHHC24 affects the protein stability of B7H3. We found that knockdown of ZDHHC24 accelerated the degradation of B7H3 protein, indicating that ZDHHC24 enhances the stability of B7H3 (Response Figure.7a-b; Fig. 4G-4H in the manuscript). We appreciate your valuable suggestion, which enabled us to further elucidate the regulatory role of ZDHHC24 in our study.
Response Figure 7. Knockdown of ZDHHC24 reduces the stability of B7H3
Q4: As they mentioned, E-peptide works through interrupting the binding of B7H3 and ZDHHC24. They should give more details about the working mechanism. For example, whether E-peptide binds with ZDHHC24? If so, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay should be utilized to obtain kinetic parameters. Besides, whether E-peptide enhances the binding of B7H3 with p62 should be detected.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this thoughtful and constructive comment. In line with your suggestion, we conducted a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay to assess the direct interaction between the E-peptide and ZDHHC24. The results confirmed that the E-peptide binds directly to ZDHHC24 with measurable kinetic parameters, supporting our proposed model (Response Figure.8a; Fig. S7D in the manuscript). Furthermore, we examined whether E-peptide treatment affects the interaction between B7H3 and p62. Co-immunoprecipitation analysis revealed that E-peptide treatment enhanced the association between B7H3 and p62 (Response Figure.8b; Fig. 7J in the manuscript). These findings are consistent with our hypothesis that the E-peptide disrupts the interaction between B7H3 and ZDHHC24, thereby reducing B7H3 palmitoylation and promoting its binding to p62. We sincerely appreciate your insightful suggestions, which greatly enhanced the mechanistic depth and experimental rigor of our work.
Response Figure 8. E-peptide binds to ZDHHC24 and enhances the interaction between B7H3 and p62.
Q5: The authors have tested the anti-tumor effect of E-peptide synthesized according to the human B7H3 amino acids sequence in the mouse tumor models. Is there significant sequence conservation of this peptide segment between humans and mice? It is necessary to verify whether the E-peptide reduces the protein expression of B7H3 and impacts its palmitoylation in mice tumors. To enhance the clinical relevance of the results, it is recommended to evaluate the anti-tumor effects of the peptide using immunologically reconstituted humanized mice.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your insightful and constructive comment. As you correctly pointed out, it is important to evaluate the sequence conservation of the E-peptide between humans and mice. We compared this region using the UniProt database and found that it exhibits a high degree of sequence conservation between the two species (Response Figure 9a). We acknowledge that this point was not clearly highlighted in the original version of the manuscript. To avoid potential misunderstanding, we have now added explicit annotations and explanatory text (Page 15, line 441-443) in the revised manuscript to clarify this rationale. Following your recommendation, we conducted additional experiments to assess the effect of E-peptide on B7H3 expression and palmitoylation in mouse tumors. The results showed that treatment with the E-peptide led to a marked reduction in both B7H3 protein levels and its palmitoylation status in mouse tumor tissues (Response Figure 9b–9c; Fig. S8L-S8M in the manuscript). Furthermore, to enhance the clinical relevance of our findings, we evaluated the anti-tumor efficacy of the E-peptide in immunologically reconstituted humanized mice. Specifically, human hematopoietic stem cells derived from umbilical cord blood were transplanted into C-NKG mice via the superficial temporal vein. After 12 weeks, successful engraftment was confirmed by flow cytometric analysis of human immune cell markers in retro-orbital blood samples (Response Figure 9d; Fig. 8M in the manuscript). Humanized mice were then subcutaneously inoculated with human colorectal cancer cells (SW480), and treated with either C-peptide or E-peptide (administered four times). The E-peptide significantly inhibited tumor growth (Response Figure 9e–9g; Fig. 8N-8P in the manuscript), increased the infiltration of CD8+ T cells (Response Figure 9h–9i; Fig. 8Q-8R in the manuscript), and markedly enhanced the expression of cytotoxic effector molecules GZMB and IFN-γ within the tumor microenvironment (Response Figure 9j–9m; Fig. 8S-8V in the manuscript). Together with our previous results in immunocompetent mice, these findings confirm that the E-peptide exhibits anti-tumor activity in both murine and humanized immune environments. We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful suggestions, which have helped us to strengthen the translational value and mechanistic depth of our study.
Response Figure 9. E-peptide reduces B7H3 expression and palmitoylation in mouse tumors and exhibits anti-tumor activity in humanized mice.
Minor comments:
Q1: In Figure 5, the authors investigated the tumor-promoting role of ZDHHC24 in the AOM/DSS-induced CRC mouse model using ZDHHC transgenic mice. However, since they have not confirmed that ZDHHC24 functions through palmitoylating B7H3 in this model, this section appears somewhat disconnected from the central topic. It is recommended to either relocate this part to the supplementary material or provide additional evidence linking ZDHHC24's activity to B7H3 palmitoylation to maintain coherence with the main narrative.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comment. In our study, ZDHHC24 serves as the palmitoyltransferase that catalyzes the palmitoylation of B7H3, a modification we found to be crucial for maintaining B7H3 protein stability. To our knowledge, the role of ZDHHC24 in colorectal cancer has not been previously reported, making it a novel and mechanistically important focus of our work. Based on this, we believe that investigating its function in an in vivo CRC model is necessary and relevant to the main theme of the manuscript. As you rightly pointed out, our original manuscript did not provide direct evidence linking ZDHHC24 activity to B7H3 palmitoylation in the AOM/DSS-induced CRC model, which could weaken the connection between this part and the central narrative. In response to your suggestion, we conducted additional experiments using this model. After successful induction of CRC, we collected tumor tissues from Zdhhc24△IEC and control mice, and assessed B7H3 protein expression and palmitoylation levels. The results showed that both B7H3 expression and its palmitoylation were reduced in Zdhhc24△IEC mice (Response Figure 10a–b; Fig. S5H-S5I in the manuscript), highlighting the in vivo relevance of ZDHHC24 in modulating B7H3 function, thereby reinforcing the study’s core mechanistic framework. We truly appreciate your valuable feedback, which helped us clarify and strengthen this section.
Response Figure 10. Loss of Zdhhc24 reduces B7H3 expression and palmitoylation in the AOM/DSS-induced colorectal cancer model.
Q2: To make sure whether ZDHHC24 interrupt the interaction of B7H3 with p62, proximity ligation assay should also be used besides Co-IP assay.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your insightful suggestion. As you recommended, we performed additional experiments to validate whether ZDHHC24 interferes with the interaction between B7H3 and p62. First, immunofluorescence staining and confocal microscopy showed that knockdown of ZDHHC24 led to increased co-localization and puncta formation of B7H3 and p62 (SQSTM1) (Response Figure 11a; Fig. 4L in the manuscript). To further validate this observation, we performed a proximity ligation assay (PLA), which provides direct evidence of protein–protein interactions. The PLA results confirmed that the interaction between B7H3 and p62 was significantly enhanced following ZDHHC24 knockdown (Response Figure 11b; Fig. 4M in the manuscript). We sincerely appreciate your valuable recommendation, which helped us reinforce the mechanistic insights of our study.
Response Figure 11. ZDHHC24 knockdown enhances the interaction between B7H3 and p62.
Reviewer #3:
It this manuscript Rao et al. have analysed a member of the B7 family and found that B7H3 shows increased expression in MSS tumours. They go on showing that B7H3 undergoes S-acylation on Cys-496, and that this slows down the turnover rate of B7H3. They propose that degradation of the non-acylated form occurs via autophagy. They show that ZDHHC24 is the major acyltransferase involved in modifying B7H3. They subsequently address the role of B7H3 acylation in tumour progression and finally design a peptide that inhibits B7H3 acylation, showing that it inhibits tumour growth.
The finding that preventing B7H3 acylation can have therapeutic benefit is clearly of interest. However the manuscript lack a rigour of thinking/writing that affects its quality.
I have focused my review on S-acylation, since the cancer immunology aspects are outside of my expertise. I do wish to mention that the effects of the e-peptide and anti-PD-1 antibodies by no means seem synergistic. The data indicates that they are somewhat additive, although not fully. From my perspective, the paper is written in a manner that is superficial and lacks the necessary rigour to make the reader confident of the quality of the work. Reference to the literature and what is really demonstrated in the literature is insufficient and again superficial. While clearly the interest of the authors lies in the therapeutic application, I regret that there is no questioning regarding the mechanistic aspect. This gives the impression of a pseudo-mechanistic insight.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your careful and detailed evaluation of our manuscript, and for noting the potential therapeutic interest of targeting B7H3 palmitoylation. We fully acknowledge your concerns regarding the need for greater scientific rigour, particularly in mechanistic depth and clarity of presentation. Following your suggestions, we have substantially revised the Introduction and Discussion sections to improve the manuscript’s structure, clarity, and logical flow. We have also strengthened the mechanistic narrative by incorporating additional experimental data, and expanded the discussion of B7H3 palmitoylation within the context of relevant literature to better frame our findings. Moreover, we have explicitly acknowledged the limitations of our study and proposed directions for future investigation. We sincerely hope that these revisions and the efforts we have made based on your suggestions will meet with your approval. We also greatly appreciate your insightful observation regarding the combined effect of the E-peptide and anti-PD-1 therapy. To further clarify this point, we have provided a brief mechanistic rationale and quantitative analysis of their interaction. Mechanistically, the E-peptide disrupts the interaction between B7H3 and ZDHHC24, leading to reduced palmitoylation and surface expression of B7H3, thereby relieving the immunosuppressive signal delivered by B7H3 to CD8⁺ T cells. In contrast, anti-PD-1 therapy directly reinvigorates CD8⁺ T cells by blocking the inhibitory PD-1/PD-L1 pathway. Although both interventions enhance CD8⁺ T cell function via distinct upstream mechanisms converging on the same effector population, our quantitative analyses indicate that their combined effects exceed simple additivity. Specifically, survival data (Fig.9G) show that the mean survival in the IgG group was 18.1 days, compared to 24.4 days for the anti-PD-1 group (a 34.8% increase) and 25.2 days for the E-peptide group (a 39.2% increase). The combination therapy extended mean survival to 40.5 days (~124% improvement over IgG). We applied the Bliss independence model—a standard approach for quantifying interaction effects under the assumption of independent action—to estimate the expected additive outcome based on the effects of each intervention alone. This analysis indicated that the expected additive improvement would be approximately 60.4%, corresponding to a predicted mean survival of 29.0 days. The observed survival benefit of the combination therapy therefore substantially exceeds the predicted additive effect, consistent with a synergistic interaction. Similarly, Bliss independence analysis shows that reductions in tumor volume (Fig.9H) in the combination group exceed predicted additive effects, supporting a synergistic enhancement of anti-tumor immunity. Taken together, these findings are consistent with a synergistic interaction between E-peptide and anti-PD-1 therapy in improving therapeutic outcomes. We hope the additional analyses and explanations help to clarify the potential mechanistic and functional interplay between these two interventions. While our initial focus was primarily on the therapeutic potential of targeting B7H3, we fully agree that mechanistic rigor is essential for a convincing scientific argument. Your comments have been invaluable in guiding these improvements, and we are truly grateful for your thoughtful feedback.
Q1: Line 38: p62 is not a cargo protein.
Response: Thank you very much for pointing this out. We agree that the term "cargo protein" was not used accurately in this context. P62 (also known as SQSTM1) is more appropriately described as a selective autophagy receptor, which binds to ubiquitinated proteins and facilitates their delivery to the autophagosome for degradation. We have revised the wording in the manuscript to reflect this distinction more precisely and now refer to p62 as an “autophagy adaptor protein” instead of a cargo protein (Page 2, line 38). We appreciate your correction, which helped us improve the accuracy of our terminology.
Q2: Line 51: for non-experts, having three acronyms in the first sentence is difficult.
Response: We sincerely thank you for the constructive suggestion. We fully agree that using multiple acronyms in the opening sentence may hinder readability for non-expert readers. To address this, we have revised the sentence in the revised manuscript to spell out the full names upon first mention. The revised sentence now reads: “Immune checkpoints, such as programmed death-1 (PD-1), programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4), play a crucial role in maintaining self-tolerance and regulating anti-cancer immunity.” (Page 2, line 52-55). We hope this change improves clarity and accessibility. Thank you again for pointing this out.
Q3: Define B7 family, provide some background information.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have added a brief definition and background of the B7 family in the Introduction (Page 3, line 64-66) to address this comment. Specifically, we included the following sentence: “The B7 family, comprising a group of structurally related transmembrane proteins, including B7-1, B7-2, B7-H1 (PD-L1), B7-H3, and others, interact with CD28 family receptors to either stimulate or suppress immune activity”. We sincerely appreciate your helpful suggestion, which allowed us to improve the clarity and completeness of the background information in our manuscript.
Q4: - Line 70: I think that what the author call “membrane localization” is plasma membrane localization”. Indeed, B7H3 is a transmembrane protein, that’s what determines its membrane localization.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this helpful suggestion. We agree that the term “membrane localization” could be misleading or too broad in this context, as B7-H3 is a type I transmembrane protein whose immunosuppressive function depends on its stable expression on the plasma membrane, rather than on intracellular membranes. In line with the your comment and the original reference (PMID: 33976130), we have revised the sentence to more accurately reflect this mechanism (Page 3, line 74-77). The revised sentence now reads: “While phosphorylation and ubiquitination sites have been predicted, N-glycosylation plays a pivotal role in stabilizing B7H3 and ensuring its stable expression on the plasma membrane, thereby facilitating its immunosuppressive function.” We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading and constructive feedback, which has helped us improve the clarity and precision of our manuscript.
Q5: Line 78: the correct term is S-acylation, often referred to as S-palmitoylation , or just Palmitoylation.
Response: Thank you for your correction. We acknowledge that “S-acylation” is the more accurate and comprehensive term, with “S-palmitoylation” or “palmitoylation” being commonly used to describe the most prevalent form of this modification. In response to your suggestion, we have revised the sentence to improve clarity and terminology accuracy. Specifically, we have replaced “Palmitoylation (usually referred to as S-palmitoylation)” with “S-acylation (often referred to as S-palmitoylation or simply palmitoylation)” in the manuscript (Page 3, line 82). We appreciate your helpful feedback, which has helped us to refine the scientific language of the manuscript.
Q6: Line 79: there is very little evidence so far that S-acylation affects protein structure. This is thus incorrect.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important and constructive comment. Our original intention was to describe the biochemical nature of palmitoylation, specifically the formation of a thioester bond between the sulfhydryl group of a cysteine residue and a 16-carbon palmitate molecule. While some studies report that S-acylation can directly or indirectly induce conformational changes. For example, S-acylation has been shown to regulate the opening and closing of membrane channels[1–3], or modulate the exit of LRP6 from the endoplasmic reticulum by tilting transmembrane domains[4]. However, we acknowledge that the phrase “is commonly used to modify protein structure” may be misleading. To avoid this ambiguity and improve scientific accuracy, we have removed the phrase from the sentence. The revised version (Page 3, line 82-85) now reads: “S-acylation (often referred to as S-palmitoylation or simply palmitoylation) is an important post-translational modification in which a thioester bond is formed between the sulfhydryl group of a cysteine residue and, most commonly, a 16-carbon palmitate.” We appreciate your careful reading and helpful feedback, which have helped us enhance the clarity and precision of our manuscript.
Reference:
[1] F B, M M, KJ S. Palmitoylation Influences the Function and Pharmacology of Sodium Channels[J]. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 2011, 108(50).
[2] Z P, Y X, J M, et al. Cardiac Sodium Channel Palmitoylation Regulates Channel Availability and Myocyte Excitability with Implications for Arrhythmia Generation[J]. Nat Commun, 2016, 7.
[3] S C, C V R, A B G, et al. Palmitoylation of Voltage-Gated Ion Channels[J]. Int J Mol Sci, 2022, 23(16).
[4] L A, B K, I I, et al. Palmitoylation and Ubiquitination Regulate Exit of the Wnt Signaling Protein LRP6 from the Endoplasmic Reticulum[J]. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 2008, 105(14).
Q7: Line 87: reword “irreplaceable”, this is likely true for any PTM.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that the term “irreplaceable” may overstate the specificity of palmitoylation, as many post-translational modifications (PTMs) contribute uniquely to immune regulation. To improve precision and avoid overgeneralization, we have replaced the word “irreplaceable” with “important” (Page 3, line 90) to avoid overstatement and improve accuracy. We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading and helpful suggestion, which has helped us refine the clarity and balance.
Q8: Abstract and lines 95, 163 and others places in the manuscript: Palmitic acid does not “mediate” palmitoylation in the context of this work, but triggers it. All palmitoylation is by definition palmitate-mediated.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We understand that the term “palmitic acid-mediated palmitoylation” could be confusing, as palmitoylation is enzymatically catalyzed and palmitic acid serves as the lipid donor rather than the direct mediator. Our original intention was to convey that palmitic acid functions as an upstream stimulus that increases B7H3 palmitoylation, rather than being the direct enzymatic mediator of the modification. In accordance with your suggestion, we have carefully revised the text in the Abstract and throughout the manuscript (Title, Abstract, Lines 99, 122, 161, 181, 558, 561, and 635), replacing “mediates” with the more appropriate term such as “triggers,” “promotes,” or “facilitates”, depending on the context, in order to ensure scientific clarity and precision. We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful feedback, which has helped improve the accuracy of our terminology.
Q9: Line 155: separating cytosolic from membrane by fractionnation when looking at a membrane protein seems rather meaning less. These type of experiments seed doubts in the reader’s mind as to the mechanistic understanding of the authors regarding the protein under study.
Response: Thank you for your valuable and critical comment. We fully recognize that B7H3 is a type I transmembrane protein. However, our rationale for performing cytoplasmic and membrane fractionation assays was not to confirm its localization, but rather to understand the mechanism behind the observed reduction in B7H3 protein levels following palmitoylation inhibition. By altering the hydrophobicity of proteins, palmitoylation can influence their stability, intracellular trafficking, functional activity, and plasma membrane localization[1–3]. We hypothesized that the reduced total B7H3 levels after 2-BP treatment could result either from mislocalization—such as impaired membrane targeting and cytosolic accumulation—or from a global degradation of B7H3 across both compartments. To distinguish between these possibilities, we conducted cytoplasmic and membrane fractionation assays. Our results showed that 2-BP treatment led to a consistent decrease in B7H3 levels in both membrane and cytosolic fractions (Fig. S1S), indicating that the loss is not due to redistribution but reflects an overall downregulation of the protein. We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful comment, which allowed us to clarify the experimental rationale and strengthen the mechanistic interpretation of our findings.
Reference:
[1] LU Y, ZHENG Y, COYAUD É, et al. Palmitoylation of NOD1 and NOD2 Is Required for Bacterial Sensing[J]. Science (New York, N.Y.), 2019, 366(6464): 460–467.

[3] S MESQUITA F, ABRAMI L, LINDER M E, et al. Mechanisms and Functions of Protein S-Acylation[J]. Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology, 2024, 25(6): 488–509.
Q10: Line 160: the authors are monitoring total B7H3 levels, not palmitoylated B7H3. This is an interpretation of the data, not a description.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that it is necessary to distinguish between total B7H3 levels and palmitoylated B7H3. You are absolutely right that the experiments shown in Figures 1K and 1L assessed total B7H3 protein levels under DMSO and 2-BP treatment conditions, rather than directly quantifying the palmitoylated form of B7H3. Our original intent was to evaluate how inhibition of palmitoylation affects B7H3 protein stability over time. Given that 2-BP is a well-established inhibitor of palmitoylation, and B7H3 is expected to be palmitoylated under DMSO treatment, we initially described the observation as a comparison of degradation rates between palmitoylated and palmitoylation-impaired (2-BP-treated) B7H3. However, we agree with you that this wording could be misleading, as it implies that the assay directly measured palmitoylated B7H3. To address this concern and more objectively describe the experimental result, we have revised the wording (Page 6, line 179-180) to read: “Treatment with 2-BP markedly accelerated B7H3 degradation (Fig. 1L and 1M)” We sincerely appreciate your careful reading and constructive feedback, which has helped us improve the accuracy and clarity of our manuscript.
Q11: Line 166: the two protein degradation “sites” in the cell are lysosomes and the proteasome. Autophagy is a pathway to lysosomal degradation. However, the default routes for a transmembrane protein like B7H3 are 1) the proteasome if it fails to fold properly during its biogenesis in the ER (this requires retro translocation as part of the ERAD pathway) and 2) trafficking to lysosomes. Given its role in the interaction with T-cells, B7H3 acts at the plasma membrane and thus its route to degradation would be endocytosis and trafficking to lysosomes via the classical route. Autophagy is not the most evident pathways as opposed to what the authors suggest, and thus the approach appears to have a significant bias. That acylation affects the endocytosis of plasma membrane transmembrane proteins has been shown for a variety of proteins. B7H3 is likely to be as others surface proteins, its endocytosis is negatively regulated by S-acylation, thus acylation deficient mutants will undergo accelerated endocytosis and lysosomal degradation. There is a priori no need to bring up autophagy.
Response: Thank you for this insightful comment. We agree that most transmembrane proteins are normally cleared via endocytosis and lysosomal trafficking or by ERAD/proteasome when misfolded. However, emerging evidence suggests that certain plasma membrane–localized transmembrane proteins can also undergo degradation via selective autophagy under specific conditions. For example, Yamamoto et al. demonstrated that the major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) (Single-pass type I membrane protein) is degraded via a selective autophagy pathway in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma[1]. Similarly, Liu et al. reported that PD-L1 (a type-I transmembrane glycoprotein) can undergo selective autophagic degradation mediated by the cargo receptor p62/SQSTM1[2]. Notably, Zhang et al. showed that demonstrated that B7H3 is degraded via selective autophagy in glioma cells, as its degradation was blocked by autophagy inhibitors and involved interaction with p62 through LC3-interacting region motifs[3]. These studies indicate that autophagy can target plasma membrane proteins in certain contexts. Our findings are consistent with these observations. In the original manuscript, we showed that treatment with 3-MA (an autophagy inhibitor that blocks the formation of the phagophore by inhibiting class III PI3K) rescued the reduction of B7H3 levels induced by 2-BP (Fig. 2A), suggesting the involvement of autophagy in B7H3 degradation. To further confirm this, we conducted further experiments to validate that B7H3 degradation occurs via the autophagy pathway. Specifically, we found that treatment with rapamycin—which inhibits mTORC1 activity and thereby induces autophagy—led to a marked reduction of B7H3 protein levels in RKOWT cells (Response Figure 12a; Fig. S2K in the manuscript). Conversely, inhibition of autophagy using 3-MA (a PI3K inhibitor that blocks autophagosome formation), bafilomycin A1, or chloroquine (both of which disrupt lysosomal acidification and block autophagic flux) effectively prevented the degradation of B7H3 in the palmitoylation-deficient mutant RKOC496A cells (Response Figure 12b; Fig. S2L in the manuscript). These results strongly support our conclusion that B7H3 is subject to degradation via the autophagy–lysosome pathway in our system. While we fully acknowledge that S-acylation can influence endocytosis, such as PD-L1[4], we believe that in our context, autophagy plays a significant and experimentally validated role. We appreciate your thoughtful comment, which prompted us to provide a more thorough explanation.
Response Figure 12. B7H3 undergoes autophagy-mediated degradation in RKO cells.
Reference:
[1] YAMAMOTO K, VENIDA A, YANO J, et al. Autophagy Promotes Immune Evasion of Pancreatic Cancer by Degrading MHC-I[J]. Nature, 2020, 581(7806): 100–105.
[2] LIU D, LI M, ZHAO Z, et al. Targeting the TRIM14/USP14 Axis Enhances Immunotherapy Efficacy by Inducing Autophagic Degradation of PD-L1[J]. Cancer Research, 2024, 84(17): 2806–2819.
[3] ZHANG M, ZHANG H, FU M, et al. The Inhibition of B7H3 by 2-HG Accumulation Is Associated With Downregulation of VEGFA in IDH Mutated Gliomas[J]. Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology, 2021, 9.
[4] H Y, J L, C L, et al. Inhibiting PD-L1 Palmitoylation Enhances T-Cell Immune Responses against Tumours[J]. Nature biomedical engineering, 2019, 3(4).
Q12: - line 170: Baf A1 and chloroquine are not autophagy inhibitors, they affect the pH of lysosomes, thus inhibit lysosomal enzymes, thus affect the end point of autophagy.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this insightful comment. You are absolutely right that Bafilomycin A1 and chloroquine do not inhibit autophagy initiation directly. Instead, they interfere with lysosomal acidification, thereby impairing the activity of lysosomal enzymes and blocking the terminal stage of autophagy. In our original text, we used the term “autophagy inhibitors” in a broad sense, which may have unintentionally caused confusion about their precise mode of action. In response to your suggestion, we have revised the sentence to more accurately reflect the mechanisms of these compounds. The updated sentence now reads: “Interestingly, pharmacological agents that disrupt different stages of the autophagy pathway—3-MA (an early-stage autophagy inhibitor), and BafA1 and chloroquine (which impair lysosomal degradation)—effectively blocked the 2-BP-induced degradation of B7H3, whereas the proteasome inhibitor MG132 had no such effect.” (Page 7, line 191-195). Thank you again for helping us improve the accuracy and clarity of our manuscript.
Q13: - Line 193: C496A has a mutation of te acylation site, not a deletion.
Response: Thank you very much for your careful reading and valuable comment. You are absolutely right—referring to the C496A mutant as having a “deletion” of the palmitoylation site was inaccurate, as the site was mutated rather than deleted. In response to your suggestion, we have corrected the description by replacing “deletion” with “mutation” to accurately reflect that C496A is a point mutant of the acylation site (Page 8, line 219). We truly appreciate your attention to detail and thank you again for helping us improve the precision of our manuscript.

You are absolutely right that confocal microscopy alone does not directly measure binding affinity, and our original wording may have overstated the interpretation of the imaging data. In response to your suggestion, we have revised the sentence to describe the microscopy results more accurately, focusing on the observed colocalization patterns rather than implying a direct binding interaction. The updated sentence now reads: “Moreover, confocal microscopy revealed that RKOC496A cells displayed greater colocalization of B7H3 with LC3 and formed more distinct B7H3–SQSTM1/p62 aggregates compared with RKOWT cells.” (Page 8, line 233-235). We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful feedback, which helped us improve the accuracy and clarity of our description.
Q15: - Line 272: ZDHHC24 has been reported to be an ER localized acyltransferase. The authors should comment on the fact that their localization at the plasma membrane is in disagreement with the literature. Also a quantification of the localization would be required.
Response: Thank you very much for your valuable comment. As you rightly pointed out, ZDHHC24 has been previously reported by Bu et al. to localize predominantly to the endoplasmic reticulum[1]. However, their study also detected partial localization at the plasma membrane, which is consistent with our findings in Figure 4B. In our study, we observed endogenous ZDHHC24 localization at both the plasma membrane and in the cytoplasm of RKO tumor cells. This distribution aligns with Bu et al.’s results, although they described prominent cytoplasmic aggregates that may result from ZDHHC24 overexpression in 293T cells. In contrast, our analysis was conducted under endogenous expression conditions, which may better reflect its physiological localization in cancer cells. Furthermore, subcellular annotations from UniProt (Q6UX98) support the possibility of multi-compartment localization: the UniProt annotation indicates localization to the plasma membrane (Response Figure 13a), while the Gene Ontology (GO) annotation suggests localization to the ER and Golgi apparatus (Response Figure 13b). This dual annotation supports our observation of ZDHHC24 presence in both the cytoplasm and plasma membrane, and suggests that its localization may vary depending on cellular context. In response to your suggestion, we repeated the confocal microscopy experiments and confirmed the co-localization of ZDHHC24 and B7H3 in both the cytoplasm and plasma membrane (Response Figure 13c). To quantitatively support these findings, we performed fluorescence intensity profile analysis of the merged signals (Response Figure 13d). These results provide further evidence that ZDHHC24 is not restricted to the endoplasmic reticulum and may function at multiple subcellular compartments, including the plasma membrane. We appreciate your thoughtful feedback, which helped us strengthen our manuscript.

Q1: - The authors discussed the rationale of the design of the “E-peptide”, in which the amino acids 488-497 in the B7H3 sequence were found to be essential for the interaction with ZDHHHC24. However, the rationale of the “C-peptide” is not explained. Why did the authors use this sequence? As you correctly noted, the E-peptide corresponds to amino acids 488–497 of B7H3, which we identified as essential for binding to ZDHHC24. To generate a proper control, we designed the C-peptide by randomly scrambling the amino acid sequence of the 488–497 region. Q2: - Did the authors check if the C-peptide is also internalized by confocal microscopy?
Response: Thank you very much for your insightful comment. Initially, we assumed that the cellular uptake of both peptides would primarily rely on the TAT transduction domain, and therefore only assessed the internalization of the E-peptide. We acknowledge that this assumption was not sufficiently rigorous. In response to your suggestion, we have now performed confocal microscopy to examine the internalization of the C-peptide as well. Q3: -The authors should provide the synthesis protocol and characterization for all the compounds, including the data that supports the assignment of structure (NMR and mass spectrometry) and purity, such as HPLC.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your insightful suggestion. We have now included the synthesis protocol for the peptide in the revised Methods section of the supplement information (Page 13, Line 369-381). The synthesis steps for the peptides are as follows: The C-peptide (YGRKKRRQRRRRKWEISQCKC) and E-peptide (YGRKKRRQRRRCWRKIKQSCE) were synthesized by QYAOBlO (ChinaPeptides Co., Ltd.) using standard Fmoc-based solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) protocols on 2-chlorotrityl chloride resin. Briefly, after resin swelling in DMF (15 mL/g, 1 h), the first Fmoc-protected amino acid (C-terminal residue) was coupled using 3 equivalents of amino acid and 10 equivalents of DIEA, followed by methanol capping. Fmoc deprotection was carried out with 20% piperidine in DMF in two steps (5 min + 15 min). After each coupling and deprotection step, a Kaiser test was performed to monitor the reaction progress. Each subsequent amino acid was coupled using 3 equivalents of Fmoc-amino acid, 3 equivalents of HBTU, and 10 equivalents of DIEA in DMF for 45 minutes. The synthesis proceeded from the C- to N-terminus via iterative cycles of coupling, deprotection, and washing, with reaction progress monitored by the Kaiser test. Following chain assembly, the resin was washed (DMF, DCM, methanol) and dried under vacuum. Peptides were cleaved from the resin using a cleavage cocktail (TFA:H₂O:EDT:TIS = 95:2:2:1) for 3 hours, precipitated in cold ether, washed, and dried. Crude peptides were purified by preparative RP-HPLC on a C18 column, using 0.1% TFA in water and acetonitrile as mobile phases. Final products were confirmed by mass spectrometry and analyzed for purity by analytical HPLC. Peptides with >98% purity were lyophilized and stored at –20°C. In addition, we have provided the relevant MS and HPLC data supporting the structural assignment and purity assessment of the E-peptide (Response Figure 15) and C-peptide (Response Figure 16). We appreciate your helpful comments, which have improved the clarity and completeness of our manuscript.
Response Figure 15. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of the E-peptide.
Response Figure 16. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of the C-peptide.
Q4: - What was the solvent used to prepare the solutions of E- and C- peptide?
Response: We sincerely thank you for this important question. To prepare the peptide solutions, both E- and C-peptides were first aliquoted into individual sterile EP tubes at 2 mg per tube and briefly centrifuged. We initially added 20 μL of 0.1% formic acid in water to pre-dissolve the peptide powder, followed by the addition of 1980 μL of sterile normal saline (0.9% NaCl). The mixture was then sonicated and vortexed repeatedly until the peptide was fully dissolved. The resulting solution had a final concentration of 1 mg/mL (approximately 354 μM, based on the peptide molecular weight of 2822.38 Da). If other concentrations are required, the volume of normal saline can be adjusted according to the molecular weight. All solutions were prepared fresh before use and filtered through a 0.22 μm sterile filter. We sincerely appreciate your careful and rigorous review, and thank you for raising this important point, which helped us clarify and improve the description of our experimental procedures.
Q5: - The authors tested the peptides in vivo. Was the hemocompatibility and proteolytic stability of the peptide assessed?
Also, does the peptides form aggregates? The aggregation could limit the application of larger concentrations.
Response: Thank you very much for your thoughtful and important comments. As you suggested, we assessed the hemocompatibility of the peptide using in vitro hemolysis assays as well as PT and APTT coagulation tests. The results showed that E-peptide did not cause hemolysis (Response Figure 17a-b; Fig. S8G-S8H in the manuscript) or prolong PT/APTT times (Response Figure 17c-d; Fig. S8I-S8J in the manuscript), indicating that the peptide possesses good hemocompatibility under the tested conditions. Regarding the proteolytic stability, we performed a preliminary pharmacokinetic (PK) analysis following intraperitoneal administration. At multiple time points, serum samples were collected and quantified by LC-MS. These results are summarized in the updated PK curve (Response Figure 17e), which shows that E-peptide reaches its peak plasma concentration at around 30 minutes and remains detectable for at least 6 hours. This pharmacokinetic profile suggests that E-peptide exhibits moderate in vivo stability. We acknowledge that our current knowledge in pharmacology is relatively limited, and the experiments we conducted represent only an initial assessment of the pharmacological behavior of the E-peptide. In future studies, we plan to collaborate with pharmacology experts to further optimize and comprehensively evaluate the pharmacokinetics, tissue distribution, and metabolic stability of E-peptide. Moreover, we will explore potential strategies—such as peptide modification or formulation engineering—to enhance its half-life and bioavailability. As for peptide aggregation, we fully agree that aggregation, especially at higher concentrations, could significantly impact biological activity and practical application. Due to time and experimental constraints, we were not able to perform physical characterization techniques such as dynamic light scattering (DLS), size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), or electron microscopy (TEM/AFM). Instead, we conducted full-scan LC-MS analysis at different concentrations to indirectly evaluate the aggregation behavior. However, as you may be aware, LC-MS is not ideally suited for aggregation detection since aggregates often dissociate during ionization or are poorly ionized, which can lead to underestimation. In our measurements, the dominant species was observed at 2820 Da with a high deconvolution score (DScore = 94.94), and no significant signal loss or abnormal high–molecular–weight species were detected in the mass (Da) spectrum (Response Figure 17f-i). These results suggest that the peptide exists predominantly in its monomeric form under our test conditions. However, we acknowledge that this approach cannot fully exclude the presence of weakly ionizing or transient aggregates. We truly appreciate your insightful suggestion and will consider employing orthogonal techniques such as DLS or SEC-HPLC in future studies to more thoroughly evaluate peptide aggregation behavior. Thank you again for your valuable input and support in improving our manuscript.
Response Figure 17. Evaluation of the hemocompatibility and pharmacokinetic profile of E-peptide.
Reviewer #5:
The manuscript titled "Palmitic Acid Mediated Palmitoylation of B7H3 Promotes Immune Escape" presents an important exploration into immune evasion mechanisms in MSS colorectal cancer, highlighting the palmitoylation of B7-H3 by ZDHHC24 as a critical modulator of tumor immune suppression. While the study is extensive and covers multiple experimental systems, several conceptual, methodological, and analytical aspects limit the current impact and clarity of the findings.
Response:
Thank you very much for your thoughtful and constructive overall assessment of our manuscript. We are grateful for your positive view on the significance of our study in uncovering a novel mechanism of immune evasion in MSS colorectal cancer. We also fully acknowledge the conceptual, methodological, and analytical concerns you raised. Your comments were insightful and highly valuable in helping us improve the clarity and impact of our work. In response, we have carefully revised the manuscript to address each of your concerns in detail, and we sincerely thank you for your efforts in guiding us toward a more rigorous and comprehensive presentation of our findings.
Q1: - Although the authors attribute the observed immune escape mechanism primarily to B7-H3 palmitoylation, the broader biological effects of palmitic acid are not fully addressed. Palmitic acid is a well-known inducer of ER stress, oxidative stress, activation of pro-inflammatory pathways (e.g., NF-κB, JNK), and lipotoxicity. Given that the concentration used for cell treatments (100 μM) is relatively high, there remains a concern that some of the observed effects could result from these pleiotropic actions rather than palmitoylation alone. While the manuscript includes experiments with 2-bromopalmitate (2-BP) to demonstrate palmitoylation dependence, additional controls such as genetic knockdown of ZDHHC24 or CRISPR-mediated editing of B7-H3 palmitoylation sites could more conclusively isolate the specific role of this modification.
Response:
Thank you very much for your insightful and constructive comment. We fully agree that palmitic acid exerts a variety of pleiotropic effects—such as inducing ER stress, oxidative stress, inflammation, and lipotoxicity—and that these effects could potentially confound the interpretation of immune escape mechanisms. We appreciate your concern regarding the specificity of the observed phenotype. To specifically address this issue, we employed multiple strategies to isolate the effect of B7-H3 palmitoylation from other actions of palmitic acid, as you suggested. First, we identified Cys496 as the palmitoylation site on B7H3 (Fig. 2J) and generated a C496A mutant cell line using CRISPR-Cas9 (Fig. S2I), enabling us to directly assess the functional relevance of this modification (Fig. 3). To identify the palmitoyltransferase responsible for B7H3 palmitoylation, we performed a comprehensive screening approach, which revealed ZDHHC24 as the candidate enzyme (Fig. S4A). We subsequently knocked down ZDHHC24 using shRNA (Fig. S4F and S4G) and further validated its role in vivo using intestinal epithelium-specific Zdhhc24 knockout mice (Fig. 5), confirming that ZDHHC24 mediates B7-H3 palmitoylation in this context. Importantly, we further demonstrated in Fig. 6 that the immune escape phenotype induced by ZDHHC24 was abolished in the B7H3 palmitoylation mutant background, providing strong evidence that the observed effects are indeed dependent on B7H3 palmitoylation rather than non-specific consequences of palmitic acid treatment. We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful feedback, which has helped us strengthen the mechanistic clarity and overall rigor of our study.
Q2: - The metabolomics analysis is presented without sufficient methodological clarity regarding normalization procedures or batch effect correction. Visualizations such as MDS plots, PLS-DA models with VIP scores, or clear volcano plots would help to more effectively communicate metabolic shifts between groups. Moreover, the connection between the identified metabolic changes and the functional outcomes of B7-H3 palmitoylation could be explored in greater detail to strengthen the mechanistic narrative.
Response: Thank you very much for your constructive suggestions regarding our metabolomics analysis. We appreciate your attention to the methodological clarity and the visualization of data interpretation. To minimize potential batch-related variability, all tumor samples used for metabolomic analysis were collected under identical conditions, rapidly snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at –80 °C. Importantly, all samples were processed and analyzed within a single LC-MS/MS run. Therefore, batch effect correction was not required, as the experimental design itself effectively controlled for inter-batch variation. Regarding data normalization, we applied a two-step approach. Initially, during the qualitative processing stage, normalization was performed using Progenesis QI v3.0 software (Nonlinear Dynamics, Newcastle, UK), which standardizes raw intensity values across samples. Subsequently, after preprocessing steps such as missing value imputation and filtering, log-transformation was applied to the data to further normalize the distribution and reduce heteroscedasticity. These procedures have now been more clearly described in the revised Methods section of the supplement information (Page 5-6, Line 139-179). In response to your helpful suggestion, we have now included a volcano plot to better illustrate the differential metabolites between groups (Response Figure 18a; Fig. S1I in the manuscript). Moreover, we appreciate your suggestion to further explore the mechanistic link between the observed metabolic changes and the functional consequences of B7H3 palmitoylation. While this is an important direction, we would like to note that inferring immune-related functional outcomes directly from untargeted metabolomics data has inherent limitations. Metabolomics primarily captures global small-molecule profiles, which reflect a complex interplay of metabolic processes but do not directly indicate immune cell activation states, cytokine signaling, or receptor-ligand interactions. Furthermore, standard pathway enrichment tools for metabolomics (e.g., KEGG) are less well-curated for immune-specific pathways compared to transcriptomic databases. As a result, the resolution of immunological insights derived from metabolomics data remains relatively low. Thus, we have included GSEA results based on RNA-seq data from MSS and MSI-H tumors to help link the observed metabolic alterations to the functional consequences of B7H3 palmitoylation, thereby strengthening the mechanistic narrative (Response Figure 18b; Fig. S3T in the manuscript). Once again, thank you for your valuable feedback, which helped us improve the rigor and clarity of this part of the study.
Response Figure 18. Volcano plot of metabolomics and GSEA analysis of RNA-seq comparing MSS and MSI-H tumors.

Our results show that lipid metabolism pathways, including “Long-Chain Fatty Acid Transporter Activity,” “Long-Chain Fatty Acid Binding,” and “Fatty Acid Binding,” are positively enriched in MSS tumors, indicating increased lipid metabolic activity in this group (Response Figures 19a-c; Figs. S1J-S1L in the manuscript). Regarding immune evasion, the gene set “Negative Regulation of T Cell Activation” is enriched in MSS tumors (Response Figure 19d; Fig. S3T in the manuscript), suggesting a more immunosuppressive environment. Conversely, “CD8-Positive, Alpha-Beta T Cell Differentiation” and “T Cell Receptor Signaling Pathway” are negatively enriched in MSS tumors (Response Figures 19e-f; Figs. S3U-3V in the manuscript), implying impaired cytotoxic T cell function. We sincerely appreciate your suggestion, which has helped enhance the mechanistic clarity and relevance of our study.

Q5: - In the clinical relevance section, the manuscript touches briefly on correlations between ZDHHC24 expression and patient outcomes but does not deeply explore publicly available datasets such as TCGA or CPTAC to support these findings. Q6: - Although the therapeutic E-peptide is a novel approach, the current data regarding its pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and toxicity remain limited. The authors mention minimal toxicity at doses up to 50 mg/kg, but detailed pharmacodynamic data and long-term safety evaluations are lacking. Response: Thank you very much for your insightful and forward-looking comments. We completely agree that a thorough understanding of the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term safety of the E-peptide is essential for evaluating its translational potential. In response to your suggestion, we performed a preliminary pharmacokinetic (PK) study by collecting plasma samples at multiple time points following intraperitoneal injection of E-peptide (10 mg/kg) in mice. LC-MS analysis revealed that E-peptide reached peak plasma concentration at approximately 30 minutes and remained detectable for at least 6 hours (Response Figure 22a). Regarding long-term safety evaluation, we performed a one-month short-term safety evaluation in vivo, during which E-peptide was administered at doses up to 50 mg/kg. At the working dose of 10 mg/kg, we did not observe any apparent signs of toxicity, such as mouse mortality, liver or kidney dysfunction, or histopathological abnormalities in major organs (Figure S8B-S8F). These observations suggest that the peptide exhibits an acceptable preliminary safety profile under the tested conditions. In future studies, we plan to collaborate with pharmacology experts to further investigate its PK properties, tissue distribution, and chronic safety assessment. In our current work, we also explored the therapeutic benefit of combining the E-peptide with anti–PD-1 antibodies. This combination showed significantly enhanced anti-tumor efficacy compared to monotherapy (Figure 9), supporting its potential clinical utility. As you rightly pointed out, validation in more clinically relevant models is essential. Due to time and funding constraints, we further extended our analysis to a humanized mouse model treated with E-peptide monotherapy, in which we observed a marked reduction in tumor burden compared to C-peptide (Response Figure 22b-k; Fig. 8M-8V in the manuscript). We fully agree that more detailed PK, biodistribution, and long-term toxicity studies are essential, and we are actively planning follow-up work to support the further development of this peptide-based therapeutic strategy. We sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback, which has greatly helped us refine our study and plan more comprehensive future investigations.

Response: Thank you very much for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a more comprehensive discussion of the potential redundancy or compensatory mechanisms among immune checkpoint molecules would enhance the depth of our manuscript. In the revised Discussion (Page 20-22, Line 591-634), we have now added a more in-depth exploration of these mechanisms. Specifically, we highlight that inhibition of B7H3 can lead to compensatory upregulation of PD-L1 on myeloid cells, as shown in previous studies[1, 2], and that PD-L1–negative tumors such as certain breast cancers may escape immune surveillance by upregulating B7-H4[3]. These findings underscore how alternative immunosuppressive pathways can undermine the effectiveness of monotherapies. We also elaborate on our rationale for combining the E-peptide with anti–PD-1 therapy, supported by our experimental findings showing enhanced antitumor efficacy with this combination. Furthermore, we now address the potential for synergy with CTLA-4 blockade, given its distinct role in targeting Treg-mediated suppression[1, 4], and we highlight other checkpoint targets such as LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT as promising candidates for future combinatorial approaches. These additions aim to provide a broader therapeutic perspective and emphasize the translational potential of our findings. We truly appreciate your suggestion, which helped us improve the depth and clarity of this important discussion.

Reviewer #2:

Q2: - Q9 concerns the separation of the cytosolic and membrane fractions. In the response, the rationale for performing the fractionation was “not to confirm its localization”. But lines 173- 176 on p.6 state, “Given that palmitoylation can also affect protein localization, we conducted cytoplasmic and membrane fractionation assays,…” Subcellular fractionation does not address localization in different compartments, but rather the distribution of a protein in particulate (membrane) fractions vs. the soluble (cytoplasmic) fraction. Q3: - Q11- the rebuttal makes a strong argument for focusing on autophagy vs. the endocytic pathway to the lysosome, but this information is not conveyed in the text. Response: Thank you for this thoughtful and constructive comment. We agree that our rationale for focusing on autophagy should be stated explicitly in the text. We acknowledge that our previous opening sentence (“Autophagy and the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) are two primary protein degradation pathways in eukaryotic cells”) was abrupt because it was not sufficiently connected to the surrounding context. In line with your suggestion, we added a brief bridging explanation to improve logical continuity. Specifically, we revised the first sentence to: “B7H3, as a membrane protein, can in principle be degraded via the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS), autophagy–lysosome pathway, or endocytosis to lysosomes (Page 7, line 187-189).” We then briefly clarify why our data support the autophagy–lysosome pathway as the predominant route in our system: 3-MA (which inhibits class III PI3K and blocks autophagosome initiation), and bafilomycin A1/chloroquine (which block lysosomal degradation) blocked the 2-BP–induced degradation of B7H3 (Page 7, line 191-195). Moreover, EBSS-induced autophagy also accelerated its degradation (Page 7, line 195-197). Therefore, we conclude that in our system, B7H3 degradation is predominantly mediated by the autophagy–lysosome pathway (Page 7, line 197-199). We are sincerely grateful for your guidance, and it has substantially improved the clarity, rigor, and readability of this section.
